newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Japan steam coal demand to jump, says EPDC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Japan steam coal demand to jump, says EPDC.

text.p: Japan's annual steam coal requirement will jump 32 million tonnes in fiscal year 2005 from the 55 million imported in 1995, Kazuo Sugiyama, consultant to the Electric Power Development Co Ltd (EPDC), said on Tuesday.

With the Japanese economy showing signs of moderate recovery, it was projected that Japan's steam coal consumption in the power sector would grow at an average annual rate of 6.8 percent in the next decade to year 2005, Sugiyama told the Japan-Australia Business Cooperation Committees meeting here.
Australia supplies 60 percent of Japan's steaming coal, exporting 34.53 million tonnes in calendar 1995, with about 30.0 million tonnes of that for the power sector.
Sugiyama expressed concern about rapid growth in energy demand in Asian countries, where total gross domestic product was growing twice as fast as the rest of the world.
Asia-wide demand for coal was predicted to grow at an average annual rate of 4.3 percent in the period to year 2000 and 3.9 percent from year 2000 to 2010, he said.
"Under these circumstances, the challenges facing the current coal market are to expand its supply capacity and maintain the balance between coal supply and demand," he said.
"We hope that Australia will develop its supply capacity."
Japanese total final energy consumption was projected to expand at an average annual growth rate of 0.9 percent in the period to fiscal 2010, he said.

Australia's total mineral fuel exports to Japan in 1995 amounted to US$5.062 billion, with coal, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and petroleum accounting for 65 percent, 25.1 percent and 8.1 percent of the total respectively. Australia supplied 9.5
percent of Japan's total mineral fuel imports in 1995, he said.
Japanese LNG demand in fiscal year 2000 and 2010 were forecast to rise to 53 million tonnes and 58 million tonnes respectively, from 42.91 million tonnes in fiscal 1995.
Australia has a 16.5 percent share of Japan's LNG market, against 40.4 percent by Indonesia.
Australia's Northwest Shelf LNG project last week announced plans to spend A$6.0 billion to expand production, mainly for exports to Japan.
Sugiyama encouraged Australia to proceed with the development of its natural gas resources.
He warned, however, that it would be difficult to justify the viability of further LNG projects.
Japan's policy of reducing its dependence on oil had remained unchanged since the oil crisis, he said.
The current goal was to reduce oil's share of primary energy supply to 52.9 percent in year 2000 and to 47.7 percent in year 23010 from 57.4 percent in 1994.

Despite popular opposition to further development of nuclear power stations in Japan, nuclear power remained a key energy source which presently provided 21 percent of installed generation capacity and 34 percent of all electricity generated,
he said. It was hoped that the uranium trade between Japan and Australia developed further, Sugiyama said.

Gordon Summers, director, Shell Coal Australia Ltd, said the world would have a heavy on-going reliance on fossil fuels, including coal and liquid hydrocarbons, for the next 20 or so years. "The role of Australia as energy producer and exporter should therefore be reasonably assured," he said.
He warned that average returns had been inadequate for Australian coal mines and that Indonesia had eroded the prospect for Australian mines.
But Indonesia was unlikely to win share from Australia in the future at the same rate, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
